Counter-Strike 2: The Most Overhyped Game of the Decade  Let’s get this out of the way—Counter-Strike 2 is hands down one of the worst sequels to a game ever made. I honestly don't know how people are still pretending that this game is any good. Every single person I’ve seen excited about it is just caught up in the nostalgia of the original Counter-Strike, which, let’s be real, was never that great to begin with.  First off, the "graphics" in CS2 are laughable. I mean, I get it, they tried to “modernize” the game, but all they really did was slap some new textures on the old models and call it a day. The textures are so glossy it looks like I’m playing on a child’s tablet. And don’t even get me started on the animations. They’re stiffer than a board and seem like they were copied from a late ‘90s animation textbook. It’s almost like they spent all their budget on the sound design (which is just as obnoxious, by the way) and forgot to hire anyone to actually animate the characters properly.  The core gameplay has gone backwards in the worst possible way. Gone are the tight controls that made Counter-Strike a legend. Now, it feels like you’re sliding around on ice, constantly losing control of your movement, especially when you try to aim at anything. Oh, and don’t even try to use the classic AWP. It’s been nerfed into oblivion, so now it’s basically useless unless you’re playing on a server full of people who think they’re in a fun house. You thought CS:GO had a ridiculous economy? Wait till you get a load of CS2’s economy system, where every round feels like you’re just throwing money into a pit.  But perhaps the worst part about Counter-Strike 2 is the community. I’ve never seen a more toxic group of players in my entire life. It's like Valve went out of their way to make the game as frustrating as possible for anyone who isn't already a master at it. No one is willing to help new players, and if you dare ask for advice, expect to get roasted by a group of 12-year-olds who think they’re pro players because they can spam headshots from across the map. Teamwork? Forget it. CS2 is more about trying to impress strangers than actually working together.  And let’s talk about the matchmaking system, which is somehow worse than CS:GO's. It seems like Valve decided to toss all logic out the window and pair you with people who are either way better than you or way worse. No balance whatsoever. It's honestly unbelievable that they think this is the best they could do. The frustration is real, and the fact that people still defend this disaster blows my mind.  Now, let’s dive into the absolute genius of CS2's lack of content and anti-cheat. You may be thinking, “But wait, isn’t the lack of content a problem?” Nope, think again. The game is so barebones, you don’t get distracted by unnecessary fluff. The lack of maps, game modes, and weapons means you get straight to the point: pure chaos. Who needs new content when you can replay the same tired maps over and over again? It’s a minimalist approach that really makes you appreciate the classic experience. It’s basically a tribute to the early days of gaming where you had nothing to work with but a few guns and the raw thrill of respawning over and over with no variety. Brilliant, right?  And let’s not forget about the complete lack of a proper anti-cheat system. Some might see this as a problem, but I honestly think it's the best thing about the game. No longer do you have to waste your time worrying about hackers ruining the experience. In CS2, everyone is a hacker—whether it’s with aim bots, wall hacks, or just blatant cheaters trying to ruin your day. It adds an element of unpredictability and suspense to every match. You never know if that player who just headshot you from across the map is actually good at the game or just running some cheat software. It really makes every encounter exciting because you can’t trust anything or anyone. It’s the Wild West out there, and I, for one, think that’s exactly how competitive games should be. A little chaos goes a long way!  But hey, let’s not forget the real reason why people keep playing: opening cases. And let me tell you, it’s absolutely worth it. Who needs actual gameplay when you can spend $10 to open a case and maybe—maybe—get a skin worth a fraction of what you paid for it? Forget about the fun of playing the game; the true magic happens when you spend money gambling in-game for a skin you’ll probably never use! It’s the perfect way to waste your money, while Valve laughs all the way to the bank. The thrill of getting an uncommon skin that looks exactly like every other skin in the game? You can’t put a price on that… or wait, actually, you can, and it's way too much for what you’re getting. Sure, most of the time you’ll get a grey or blue skin that looks like it was designed by someone who failed art class, but who cares when you might unlock something that looks "cool" for a split second?  In conclusion, if you’re still playing Counter-Strike 2, you’re either a masochist or you’ve already lost all sense of self-worth. The game isn’t fun, the community is unbearable, and the developers clearly don’t care about making a good game. But hey, if you enjoy being constantly let down and throwing money into a case-opening pit of despair, then I guess CS2 is perfect for you. It’s honestly a miracle this game didn’t kill the series outright.

Counter-Strike 2 – A Modern Evolution of a Classic Shooter  Counter-Strike 2 takes everything that made its predecessor a legendary competitive shooter and refines it with modern technology, improved mechanics, and a fresh visual upgrade. It’s still the fast-paced, skill-based FPS that fans love, but with smoother gameplay, better graphics, and new tactical possibilities.  Why Counter-Strike 2 is a Great Game  1. Improved Graphics and Engine Built on the Source 2 engine, CS2 offers sharper visuals, improved lighting, and more detailed environments, making classic maps feel fresh while maintaining their competitive balance.   2. Refined Movement and Shooting Mechanics The movement and shooting feel tighter and more responsive, enhancing the precision that has always defined Counter-Strike. Whether it's peeking corners or landing headshots, the game rewards skill and mastery.   3. New Smoke Grenade Physics Smoke grenades are now dynamic, reacting to gunfire and explosions. This change adds a new strategic layer, making gameplay even more unpredictable and tactical.   4. Updated Matchmaking and Tick Rate Improvements CS2 introduces sub-tick updates, reducing input delay and making the game feel more responsive, ensuring that every shot and movement registers as accurately as possible.   5. Classic CS Gameplay, Modernized At its core, Counter-Strike 2 retains what made the series great—team-based strategy, intense gunplay, and high-skill competition—while updating it for a new generation of players.    Why I Love Counter-Strike 2  1. Competitive and Rewarding Gameplay Every match feels intense and meaningful. Winning a clutch round, executing a perfect strategy, or landing a crisp headshot is always satisfying.   2. High Skill Ceiling I enjoy the challenge of improving my aim, movement, and game sense. CS2 rewards dedication, and there’s always something new to learn or refine.   3. Classic Maps with a Fresh Look Playing on legendary maps like Dust2, Mirage, and Inferno with enhanced visuals keeps the nostalgia alive while making the experience feel fresh.   4. Great for Playing with Friends Whether I’m grinding ranked matches or just having fun in casual mode, CS2 is always better with friends, fostering teamwork and communication.    Final Thoughts  Counter-Strike 2 successfully modernizes a classic, keeping the core gameplay intact while introducing meaningful improvements. The refined mechanics, enhanced visuals, and tactical depth make it an outstanding competitive shooter. For me, CS2 isn’t just a game—it’s a test of skill, strategy, and precision that keeps me coming back for more.

Counter-Strike 2 has a unique style, similar to Counter-Strike 1.5/1.6, but there are a ton of cheaters in the game. Even when I report them through support, the response is always that it's enough in-game, but I continue to lose against cheaters. This is incredibly frustrating, especially when losing points in premier.  I recommend that Premier Points and stats should not be affected when playing against cheaters. It seems like the developers don’t care about the players’ frustration, which is ruining the game. You are hurting the community.  I’ve been playing CS since 1999, but the lack of action against cheaters is disappointing. Cheaters are not being banned, and players don’t get notifications about bans, unlike games such as PUBG. Losing to cheaters feels like a waste of time.  Deathmatches and Premier mode are both filled with cheaters, and Valve’s anti-cheat system is not effective. At the very least, use AI to detect player behavior and flag potential cheaters for investigation. Watching replays makes it clear when someone is cheating.  Why do I pay the price for developers’ failure to fix cheaters? If Valve can’t fix this, at least implement a fair system, like Rainbow Six Siege, where players get points back when cheaters ruin the game. A typical match in CS2 lasts 30-50 minutes, including overtime—am I just playing to waste my time?  I want to achieve a high Premier Rank, but it's impossible when lower ping players dominate. I don’t like shooting at a player’s head when they’re not even on my screen. Ping differences are a huge problem. For instance, with 68ms, I shouldn't have to play against someone with 1ms, which gives them an unfair advantage. Recoil and hitboxes aren't the same for everyone, making the game feel unbalanced. So, whether you're playing with friends or racking up rage-inducing solo queue matches, Counter-Strike will forever have a place in your heart (or at least in your list of most-played games). PUBG is still fun to play. You can still find decent lobbies for Arcade if you love that, some events are fun (zombies). If you don't like to play against players, you have a mostly AI mode with up to 12 real players. For the most part if you are playing normal mode and dropping in, avoid areas with lots of buildings, usually for players who want a quick elimination or fast paced fighting. Each game lasts roughly 20-30 minutes if you manage to survive past the first zone. I understand that some people would want to jump straight into area with lots of people and loot but these areas are not great especially if your goal is to win. Once you land you will be competing against 2 or more teams and would probably get gunned down. You won't be able to get as much kills but you have a stronger chance to win if you land away from the hot drop zones. As you play more, you would find that your decision making and positioning become better and better, which would enable you to survive in hot zones and have an easier time getting kills. As an 8 year old game, its natural that long time players have an advantage, but they can also lose fights. For those getting into the game, play casual mode and have fun, you will get better.  Monetization: The game isn't ptw, if anything the skins make you stand out a little. Battle passes, loot boxes, and cosmetics are enticing but isn't neccesary for game play. You can get free stuff from battle passes and use the free BP that you get from playing games to buy lootboxes. You open the lootboxes for cosmetics and while not all of them are good cosmetics, you do have a chance to get something nice. Sometimes PUBG have events which have vehicle cosmetics. They are cool but also loud and requires you to stand 2 seconds to equip the skin. It's also possible to get the skin from the free lootboxes if you are lucky.

PUBG – From Battle Royale to Battle Pass Simulator  I’ve been playing PUBG since early access, back when frying pans were the best armor in the game and jumping out of a moving vehicle meant instant death. It was raw, it was broken, and it was glorious. Despite its jank, the thrill of that chicken dinner kept me coming back for over 4,400 hours—streaming, participating in community events, and witnessing some of the best and worst moments a battle royale could offer.  But after eight long years, I must admit... PUBG has finally won. Not as a refined, polished, thrilling experience. No, it won by outlasting its players, grinding us down, and mutating into something unrecognizable—a desperate, free-to-play mobile game in disguise, where the only thing dropping faster than me in Pochinki is my respect for the devs.  Battle Passes, Gambling, and the Art of Selling Out Remember when PUBG’s battle passes were actually fun? They gave meaningful rewards, they were challenging, and they made you feel like you were progressing in something other than just your debt to loot box addiction. Now, every pass is just another overpriced chore list, rehashed quests rewarding you with a currency system so complicated it probably qualifies as an economics degree.  And just when I thought the game couldn’t stoop any lower, PUBG Studios went, “Hold my G-Coin.” This year, they introduced a full-on casino aesthetic—slot machines, lucky spins, and randomized G-Coin loot boxes. This isn't even trying to hide the gambling mechanics anymore; it’s just straight-up waving a neon “Insert Credit Card” sign in your face. What started as a battle royale has become a glorified slot machine with occasional gunfights in between microtransactions.  Cheaters and Anti-Cheat: A Never-Ending Love Story Let’s talk about the real MVPs of PUBG—the cheaters. They’ve been here since the beginning, they’re more dedicated than the devs, and somehow they’re still outnumbering players in some lobbies. PUBG says they ban thousands of accounts every week, but fun fact: I still get lasered from 500m away by some dude named “FreeChickenHacks” who made his account 10 minutes ago.  Meanwhile, casual players and content creators get the cold shoulder. Want better matchmaking for newcomers? Nope. Want proper streamer support? Good luck. Want an esports revival? Forget it. PUBG Studios has made it clear: money comes first, community second, and game integrity somewhere in the negatives.  PUBG 2.0? Or Just More Broken Promises? There’s been talk of PUBG 2.0 for years, with devs hinting at major overhauls and Unreal Engine 5 upgrades. But after all this time, all we’ve seen is a mountain of paid skins and another unfinished roadmap. Rumors say something’s in the works, but knowing PUBG Studios, it’ll either be: A) Another cash grab B) Some half-baked side project no one asked for C) An actual improvement (but only available in the premium pass, obviously)  Conclusion: "A Love Story Gone Wrong" PUBG was special. Even when it was janky, frustrating, and occasionally unplayable, it had soul. The tension, the firefights, the last-circle heart-pounding moments—it was an experience. But now? Now, it’s just another corporate product, desperately clinging to life with monetization schemes and ignoring everything that made it great in the first place.  And so, after eight years, I finally have to say it: Goodbye, PUBG. It feels like breaking up with a girl I once loved... except in this case, it’s more like a divorce that went really, really wrong.  💔 10/10 memories, 2/10 current game. Would not remarry.

It was the late '90s, a time when the internet still buzzed with the sound of dial-up modems and cybercafés were sacred temples for young gamers. That’s where I first discovered Counter-Strike. Back then, it was just a Half-Life mod — a simple idea: terrorists vs. counter-terrorists. But for me, and for many from my generation, Counter-Strike was much more than that.  I remember my first matches on maps like de_dust and cs_assault. Games full of adrenaline, improvised strategies, and shouting between friends whenever someone pulled off an epic play… or died in the dumbest way. But it was also in those servers where I met the people who, without realizing it at the time, would become my best friends.  As time passed, we grew up. We studied, worked, moved away, some of us became parents. I now have several kids, responsibilities, a life that no longer revolves around spending afternoons at a LAN café. But one thing hasn’t changed: I still play Counter-Strike. Not every day, of course. Sometimes once a month, maybe twice. But always with the same friends. We log in, even if it’s just for an hour, and we’re back to being those kids from the 2000s — yelling through our headsets, laughing at silly moments, and coming up with absurd strategies that never actually work.  The most beautiful part is that now my kids watch me play, asking about that “old game” I like so much. Some of them have even started playing it too. I tell them that thanks to Counter-Strike, I have my best friends. That it was more than a game; it was a bridge between eras, a bond that’s lasted decades, a space where we’re still ourselves, no matter how much our lives change.  Counter-Strike didn’t just define a gaming era — it defined a part of my life. And as long as I can lift a mouse and hit the “buy AK-47” key, I’ll be there, in the server with my lifelong friends. Because some matches, simply, never end.

I chased red skins like they meant something. I spun the digital roulette over and over, watching gold pass me by like a cruel joke. StatTrak numbers felt like validation. And when I finally landed a knife? I felt nothing. Just a momentary high, followed by the gnawing shame of checking my bank account and wondering what I could’ve done with that rent money.  I lied to myself constantly. This is the last one. I’ll sell this and break even. I traded dignity for pixels. I knew what I was doing—and I still clicked "open case."  But the worst part? I kept playing.  Even after the debt. Even after the friendships faded. Even after the joy became anxiety. CS2 had me. Not just with the gameplay, the endless ranked grind, the false hope of global elite. But with the cruel, glittering promise of luck. The skins became my obsession. My justification. My downfall.  Counter-Strike 2 didn’t ruin my life. I handed it over willingly.  And I’ll probably log in again tonight. Just one more match. Maybe one more case.  Just one more.

CS2 is like a facelift that forgot the brain – visually nice, but dumb as hell  I wanted to like Counter-Strike 2, I really did. I’ve been playing CS since the days when your teammates would yell at you in internet cafés and call you a noob for not buying defuse kits. So when Valve said “Hey, we’re upgrading to Source 2,” I was like, okay cool, maybe we’ll finally get a fresh take on the game we love.  Turns out, CS2 is basically CS:GO Lite with RTX ON and a whole lot of things missing or broken.  The Good (yes, there’s some):  Smokes are sick now — dynamic and interactive. You can shoot through them and they react to the environment. Legit cool.  The game looks better. Cleaner maps, better lighting. Definitely prettier.  Gunplay still feels like CS… when it works.  It’s free, so I guess I can’t complain too hard, right?  But now the part where things get sh-tty  1. Hit reg is a joke. You ever die, check the kill cam, and apparently you were aiming at the floor while your cross hair was glued to their head? Yeah. That happens a lot. And I’m not even talking high ping or potato net. Something about the tick system and sub-tick feels off.  2. Performance is garbage unless you're running a NASA PC. CS:GO used to run on a calculator. CS2? My friend with a 1660 can barely hit stable frames on Dust 2 without his fans screaming for help. Huge stutters in fights, weird frame pacing, and GPU temps through the roof.  3. Where is the content??? No Danger Zone. No Arms Race. No proper Workshop support. Surf and KZ servers are either janky or straight-up gone. Even basic community servers are a mess. It’s like Valve deleted half the soul of the game and went “trust us, it’s better this way.”  4. Audio sounds like I have socks over my ears. Footsteps are inconsistent. Sometimes you can hear the enemy from Narnia, sometimes they ninja behind you and stab you in broad daylight. Directional audio is scuffed and makes it feel like I’m playing underwater. I'm using Corsair HS80, btw.  5. Matchmaking is worse somehow. Premier mode is just a weird knockoff of Valorant ranked. It doesn’t even show you actual ranks anymore. Also, cheaters are still a thing. The “new VAC” is apparently just old VAC in a new hat.  CS2 had the potential to be the next evolution of Counter-Strike. Instead, it feels like a downgrade disguised as progress. Valve took one of the most refined competitive shooters ever and turned it into a beta test with fancy lighting.  I’m not uninstalling (yet), nor will I ever do, I miss CS:GO. At least that game worked.  TL;DR: CS2 looks pretty, smokes are cool, but the game feels like an unfinished mod with hitreg problems, bad performance, missing features, and weird audio. It's CS, but worse.  Valve, pls fix.

Counter-Strike is hands down the best competitive game ever made. It's simplicity allows balance that is virtually impossible to find in any other competitive game in the gaming scene. The combination of the needed individual skill, team communication and teamwork to play at the highest levels is unmatched. For a new player, Counter-Strike is probably a daunting experience at first. The amount of skill expression seen in Counter-Strike can prove to be a steep slope to tackle as an inexperienced player facing others with hundreds if not thousands of hours played. Stick with it and you will realize that it's not about anything other than your own technical skill, knowledge and ability to work with other players that is holding you back. However, it is not a perfect game. If you don't want to face cheaters, ever, then you will probably have to play via faceit or some other client, which will be extra challenging for new players. Another thing to point out is the importance of specifically teamplay and team communications to win games, which can be lacking in the lower ranks of CS and be a source of irritation for a lot of players who want to climb the ranks. Finding players who you have good chemistry with and playing with them is a good alternative, at any rank. Furthermore there is a big incentive to gamble in order to have cool looking gun-, glove-, knife- and operator skins, which I'm personally against. I only recommend this game to non-casual players. Sure, there are a lot of community made maps and servers and whatnot, which can offer a more casual gaming experience which I have personally spent a lot of time on but Counter-Strike really shines in the simple competitive format. Whatever you want to sink your teeth into, expect to spend a lot of hours to get the gist of it.

CS2 Review: A Fresh Coat of Paint, But Is It Enough?  Counter-Strike 2 (CS2) is Valve’s long-awaited sequel to the legendary CS:GO, and while it brings some solid improvements, it’s not without controversy.    The Good:  Graphics & Engine: CS2 runs on the Source 2 engine, which gives the game a much cleaner, more modern look. Maps like Dust II and Mirage feel familiar but look sharper, with better lighting and improved textures.    Responsive Smokes: One of the standout features is the dynamic smoke system. Smokes now react to bullets and grenades, opening up fresh strategies and making gameplay feel more alive.    Tickless Servers: Valve’s new sub-tick system is meant to make hit registration more consistent. It’s a technical improvement, though some players still debate if it truly feels better in practice.    The Mixed:  Gameplay Changes: CS2 keeps the core Counter-Strike feel but makes subtle tweaks to movement and shooting. Some players feel it’s smoother, others say it’s clunkier. It depends on who you ask.    UI & Sounds: The new interface is sleeker but takes some getting used to. Weapon sounds and effects have been updated—some love them, others miss the old feel.    The Bad:  Performance & Bugs: At launch, many players reported FPS drops, stuttering, and bugs. Valve has been patching frequently, but performance still varies by system.    Missing Features: Not all content from CS:GO made it over yet. Some maps, modes, and community features are still absent, which makes it feel like CS2 isn’t fully done.    Final Verdict:  CS2 is a promising upgrade to a legendary franchise. It looks better, adds some cool tech, and keeps the core gameplay mostly intact. But it still feels like a work in progress. If you're a CS:GO veteran, you'll likely be torn between appreciating the improvements and missing what’s been lost (or hasn’t been added back yet).    Rating: 7.5/10 – Good, but still loading... Counter-Strike 2 Review: A Tactical Evolution With Mixed Results Rating: 7.5/10  After over a decade of domination by Counter-Strike: Global Offensive, Valve has finally released Counter-Strike 2, a long-awaited successor built on the Source 2 engine. While it brings undeniable visual upgrades and under-the-hood improvements, CS2 feels more like an overhaul than a true sequel—and that’s both its strength and its weakness.  Graphics and Engine Overhaul The most noticeable change is the jump to the Source 2 engine. Maps are brighter, more detailed, and have improved lighting and physics. Smoke grenades now react dynamically to gunfire and environmental changes, introducing new tactical possibilities. Animations are smoother, and weapon models look fantastic, giving the game a modern feel without sacrificing its competitive edge.  Gameplay and Mechanics Core gameplay remains unchanged—and for good reason. CS2 still thrives on precision, communication, and strategy. However, some mechanics have been refined. Movement feels slightly different (to the frustration of long-time players), and hit registration has seen improvements. Valve introduced subtick servers to enhance responsiveness, though the real-world impact has been inconsistent, and some pros argue that it hasn't lived up to expectations.  Maps and Modes Classic maps like Dust2, Mirage, and Nuke return with visual upgrades, but many players miss popular community maps and modes that haven't yet made the transition. The lack of features like Arms Race, Flying Scoutsman, or custom servers at launch disappointed a portion of the community.  UI and UX The user interface has been cleaned up and modernized. The new buy menu feels more intuitive and flexible, but also drew some criticism for breaking years of muscle memory. Stat tracking and player profiles are improved, but still somewhat barebones compared to what third-party tools offer.  Community and Transition Perhaps the most controversial part of CS2 is how Valve handled the transition. CS:GO was entirely replaced by CS2, leaving players no way to revert. Many community servers, mods, and competitive leagues were disrupted. The game is still stabilizing, and updates have been rolling out to address bugs, performance issues, and balance concerns.  Verdict Counter-Strike 2 is a promising evolution of the iconic shooter, but it feels like a work in progress. It preserves the tactical brilliance of its predecessor while modernizing its visuals and systems. However, rough edges, missing features, and a forced transition have made the launch rocky. If Valve keeps listening to the community and iterating, CS2 could easily cement itself as the future of competitive FPS. For now, it’s a solid—but not flawless—upgrade.

When I give this game a thumbs up, I give it that for people like me.  I'm an adult now, I've been around CS since I was around 11, back when CS:S was the main thing. CS:S was scattered in gameplay, didn't really have centralized matchmaking and actually trying to play the game as intended was difficult. I mainly messed around in gun game lobbies or TTT, and I mainly bought it to expand my Garry's Mod assets at the time.  Then CSGO came out, and with me being a teenager that liked shooting things I took a swing at it, and got started with Vanguard. I had played a lot of competitive FPS's up to that point but CS had hit the primal urge that all the others were born from. CSGO was in spirit the perfect sequel, and read this further if you want that to make sense.  Halo > Halo 2; H2 is regarded as one of the greatest sequels ever and the reason for that is that it innovated on already existing content of the original, added new content that kept up in spirit with the OG, and was an overall outstanding iteration on the original formula. In this sense, CSGO was the perfect sequel to whatever you could call the OG, whether it be CS:S or CS 1.6; or the combination of both (I'll let the monkeys argue over that in the comments.)  So, now I'm gonna circle back to what I said in the beginning, "When I give this game a thumbs up, I give it that for people like me."  CSGO had the innovation of proper loot cases (or whatever synonym you can come up with across other games), with skins that were unlike any other attempt at the concept (floats, wear, patterns, etc.), and this created a player-driven economy that the developers get to skim off of in their own self-created ecosystem. A concept that other publishers have tried to make poor imitations of in various ways (Just buying the skins, lesser forms of cases, etc.) In terms of innovation (or invention in this case) Valve knocked it out of the park. This is my problem though, I was 17 when I got into the game, and despite being well under gambling age, I definitely bought cases, keys, and spent many of my minimum wage fast food job paychecks fueling my desire to unbox a knife. In this aspect I think that being an adult now makes this more acceptable, but at the time not-so-much, there were better things for my 17 year old self to preoccupy himself with.  -------------------------------------------------------  This all aside, let's talk about CS2 objectively, and not from the rose-tinted glasses that many others seem to have over CSGO.  CS is one of those games that if it experiences even a minute change the community will collectively empty their bowels wherever they read the patch notes. In the car, at school, in bed, you name it, I can near-guarantee a passionate rant based out of hatred about the patch notes is soon to grace your eyes (even though they barely skimmed the notes and took to reddit to see what they should hate about it.) AK's and M4's must always be balanced this way, maps must stay predictable and anything new throws out their game sense. I'm not going to entertain these thoughts, a lot of the changes in CS2 are good, and resisting change in the first place is foolish. Everything changes, progress is constant.  The new smoke mechanics are astounding, and Valve is one of the first in the industry to attempt these new particle physics, I mean come on, people shooting through smoke giving away their location? Grenades clearing it temporarily? This adds new layers to the gameplay and most importantly the strategy, and like a perfect sequel it does it in amazing ways that doesn't compromise the spirit of what CS has going on for itself.  New additions to maps like Dust 2 have kept it interesting, the jump from CT to Cat is a great change, and it's a tasteful addition to the routes you can take to cat from A, mid, doors, CT, or even from car pushing back to CT should you not have the luxury of going down long to watch over the site. While a good portion of the community doesn't like this change, I'll tell them that it's not like they created a ladder going straight from the back of CT up to catwalk. The box jump takes time, it's risky, it's loud, and it really makes you vulnerable, the convenience to risk is balanced and that's what you have to look for when seeing if things like this are good changes.  At first I was hesitant about the armory passes, but I think that it's a good change of pace for monetization in CS. Battlepasses that aren't timelocked, you can redeem the points for a swing at anything in that dedicated store, you can have multiple of them, and the skins behind them aren't total dogwater either. Though I do wish they had stat-trak, I'm not gonna complain about a FN Long Dog should I ever finally unbox one.  The new lighting is mostly good, I think the CSGO art style was good don't get it twisted. After reviewing the before and after on Mirage for instance it is quite nice to have the inside of palace be lit up and not so dreary or dark. CS2 feels less like the source games of yore and has jumped forward with Source 2. The light bouncing and the vibes of the interiors of many of these maps has improved greatly with the new lighting. I did say mostly good, and this is because I do agree with others that it can be washed out in places. Right there at palace, the interior is nice, but once you walk out over firebox the plywood's detail is hard to see and the colors kind of blend together. I can easily see how this would cause some issues with gameplay, visibility, and being able to suss out the enemy. The skins are another issue, these skins were made for a darker world palette, and lighting too, so in cases of skins like a printstream the vibrant pearlescence is washed out and doesn't look as good as it did in CSGO. In a game where the skins are what make the majority of the money, this is problematic.  Though, I must say that the gameplay is still amazing, and the launch issues many complained about have mostly been rectified (mostly as in I can't find any of them anymore but I'm sure others will nitpick), subtick is still an issue but I don't really have this issue very often, like once every 20-30 games. It's non-consequential to me.  -------------------------------------------------------  CS2 is the perfect sequel to CSGO. The original core gameplay is here (as in nothing has been taken out), and the additions they've made have only made it better. New smokes are cash money, the map changes are pretty great too, the lighting is mostly good but struggles in other places (Reminder, Halo 2 was also like this but a bit worse in that dept.)  The reason this game is good for a person like me is that it has all the fixtures that I'd want, and that is appropriate for me. Skins/Gambling, who cares I'm in my late 20's now, I can make these decisions as a responsible adult. The strategy, gameplay, and patience required is ultimately the tempting aspects of gameplay that keep me playing it or bringing me back. The friends I play with, and the fodder I get to shoot at, are also some amazing things I enjoy about it. (Fodder as in: Impatient teenagers who hold W and don't like to think beyond 5 seconds ahead. Atleast that goes for most of you :^) )  Nostalgia vision is a bitch, and after seeing the content put out by others saying they grew up with CSGO, I get it man, I really do. I watched Halo go from peak to dogwater in a matter of a decade, I get the fear and hesitance that comes with change. The circumstances are different here, the game is great, the gameplay is fun, the skins are cool and the skills that you build here are to me pretty valuable in gaming.  CS is far from a "dead game" like many were saying before Armory pass update hit. Cheaters are everywhere and CS is unfortunately not an exception, but I am reviewing the game at its core before I am hit by a tirade of "cheaters bro cheaters" yes man, I get it, cheaters.  CS2 is a great sequel, nostalgic redditors be damned.

The bright neon maps filled me with a sense of wonder I had not felt since they were toddlers chasing after soccer balls in the yard. Each round felt alive, every echo of footsteps carried the possibility of triumph or defeat. In that moment I was not just a player seeking a quick win, I was a parent soaking in a few spare minutes of joy before bedtime stories and bedtime prayers.    The core gameplay is as tight and precise as ever, with each shot carrying weight and intention. The maps are vibrant canvases where strategy and instinct collide in the best possible way. I still marvel at the smooth transitions between rounds and the way the community rallies around a clutch play. Even now I find myself searching for that spark of excitement that once lit up our little living room, and CS2 delivers it with startling clarity.    Of course it is more than just pixels on a screen. For me the game has become a living memorial to those moments when we shared laughter and simple victories. Whenever I log in I feel them beside me, cheering me on or playfully teasing my missed grenade toss. It is a strange comfort to know that even though they are no longer here, our shared passion lives on in every match I play.    Looking ahead I see CS2 growing stronger, evolving, and drawing in new players who will create their own memories and maybe some day look back on their own simpler times. At one point this was my thing but not anymore. If it's your thing still that's cool.  I was uninstalling this and the 80gb of storage space floored me enough to write this. The original was 20gb, for reference. There's so much bloat that it caused my face to twist when I realized how much space was wasted on a game I don't play anymore. And that was when I wrote this.  Like I used to have a lot of fun playing on the original (inaccessible still) CSGO, and all of the workshop maps associated with it. Lost to time now, most of them. I used to even enjoy competitive, quite frequently too (My record was Gold Nova Master before one of the great ELO/matchmaking changes).   And I guess I got older, the game just makes me very angry now, frustration is a big driver for improvement here. But I can't say for sure what it is even that makes me feel so bad playing this game. I stopped playing roughly around when they changed most of the gun sounds, and there's been a truly extraordinary amount of updates since then.   Source 2 is also a very impressive upgrade. However for my personal taste there's something now missing from the game visual style. It feels like 2006 again when every developer got access to the bloom setting and used it so often gamers got sick of it. The UI change feels weird to me and I can't navigate the menus anymore and I don't have the inclination as it is anyway to learn where all of the buttons went.   It doesn't help that this game seems almost predatory. Skins, gambling, and real cash are permanently attached to the game now and it's been that way for a very long time. You certainly do not need them to play, but very often you will find people obsessed with skins and the skin market. I own some myself, some skins are quite pleasant looking and some offer stat tracking on the gun you have the stat track skin for.  And I deeply miss hosting my own servers and having my friends join to play Michael Myers, yknow? We'd get a bad comp match back then, and instead of going "we ball" or "run it back" we'd do something else in the game and cool before jumping back in. Now the game only feels focused on further developing this competitive community. Which I suppose is fine? Even though I feel a sense of revulsion anytime I meet someone who takes competitive CS2 seriously now, same extends to many competitive games. And I know that's a personal feeling.   I think the only thing I can take away from this is something basic, the game will not remember the people like me who played it differently. It will not remember all of the workshop maps, either. Among the missing maps were heavily scripted stories, a bank heist, a fantasy where you slay a dragon. Gone. Because CS2 needed to replace CSGO. The developers decided that both could not co-exist and thus wiped the face of the workshop clean.   The thing about those heavily scripted maps too was that I'm pretty sure the people that had made those were Russian. Those were made pre-war. Those workshop maps might be permanently lost, who knows what happened to the creator after so many years.  Remember this was Valve, by the way. Very well known for mod and community support at one point.  It's also the same Valve that let Bethesda attempt to monetize the Skyrim workshop over a decade ago now, we shouldn't forget that either and remember who to hold accountable for mistakes like this.   And I use mistake generously here. Sometimes it's not so easy to say.  Of course this entire review is based on memory, some relatively recent, I can't afford to give you a proper review of what the gameplay is like today, and it would date the review anyway. Neither can I truly explain the minutiae of how this game does not respect you nor your time. I want to say it uses the same method of keeping users that a social media platform does, keep the player irritated so that when they do improve the dopamine hits are enhanced. But that's speculative.  I don't think I've ever written a negative review for a Valve product.  I've never felt offended by anything they've done up until recently.   Must be that I'm real sick of the way we've been going for the past decade now. Maybe someone else remembers, maybe I've lost it.   I dunno, that's all I wanted to write.  ez pz lemon squeezy

I’ve been playing Counter-Strike since CS 1.3, when jumping off a box felt like parkour and buying an AWP didn’t mean you were toxic... just rich. I've crouch-walked through dust in 640x480, sprayed through walls in aztec, and lived through the trauma of CS:Source’s hitboxes. And now, here we are — CS2. A whole new chapter.  Let’s be real — CS:GO was already a masterpiece. But CS2? It’s like your favorite band released a remastered album... and also added fog, volumetric grenades, and occasionally let you fly into the sky during a bug. Progress.  Watching legends like Heaton, Potti, elemeNt, fisker, f0rest, GeT_RiGhT, JW, s1mple, and ZywOo, now Donk evolve through these versions is like watching Pokémon evolve — only with more screaming and flashbangs. I’ve aged, my hairline has receded, but my muscle memory still bunnyhops (in my dreams, anyway).  And yes, CS2 is beautiful. The gunplay is crisp, the visuals are stunning, and the buy menu? Oh, the BUY MENU. Remember when buying a deagle meant you were smart and broke? Now it feels like Wall Street: buy this, rebalance that, swap mid-game... I didn’t realize I needed an MBA to afford a loadout.  Still, every bomb plant, every last-second defuse, every accidental team flash — it’s all still Counter-Strike. The chaos. The clutch. The community (and the occasional kid with a mic louder than a flashbang). This isn't just a game — it’s my youth, my rage therapy, and my aim trainer rolled into one.  Verdict: 10/10, would get one-tapped again for nostalgia.

To jakbyś zamienił Ferrari na rower z urwanym łańcuchem i kółkami bocznymi. Ale okej, po kolei.    Silnik Source 2? Więcej jak SOUR 2, bo wszystko w tej grze jest kwaśne. Hitboxy? Jakby strzelać do duchów – raz trafiasz w nogę i robisz headshota, innym razem dasz serię w łeb i gość nadal żyje, bo "tickrate 128 na papierze, ale w duszy 30".    Ruch postaci? Jakby wszyscy mieli połamane nogi i biegali w basenie z kisielem. Movement z CS:GO był precyzyjny. Tutaj? Skaczesz jak chomik po energetykach, a bhop działa raz na pięć prób – i to przy pełni księżyca.    Dym granaty? Aaaa to jest dopiero kabaret. Te ich "dynamiczne smoki" wyglądają jak chmura z Vape’a nastolatka na TikToku. Do tego bugują się o wszystko – ściany, graczy, nawet o własne ego.    Menu? Zmienione. Na gorsze. Chciałem kupić M4 – przypadkiem wziąłem Negeva, bo interfejs wygląda jak z mobilnej wersji robionej przez stażystę.    Mapy? Wyglądają ładniej – i tylko ładniej. Bo gameplay leży i kwiczy. Dust2 świeci się jak reklama kasyna w Vegas, ale feeling? Zniknął. Mirage? Ciągle to samo, tylko teraz masz wrażenie, że patrzysz przez szkło powiększające.    Matchmaking? The new Loadout system allows players to customize their weapon selection before matches, adding a layer of strategic depth. The improved matchmaking system and server tick-rate enhancements ensure smoother and more responsive gameplay.  Community & Longevity Like its predecessor, Counter-Strike 2 thrives on its competitive scene and modding community. Whether you’re grinding ranked matches or exploring custom game modes, there’s always something to keep players engaged. However, some concerns remain about cheaters and optimization issues, which Valve will need to address to maintain a fair playing field.  Final Verdict Counter-Strike 2 is not a revolution, but rather a refinement of what made CS:GO a global phenomenon. It’s a must-play for fans of tactical shooters, offering a modernized experience while staying true to its roots. If you love high-stakes, skill-based competition, CS2 is well worth your time. 🧠 Things I've Learned from CS2:  Trust issues — Never peek first. That corner has a guy with an AWP who’s been holding the angle since the Cold War.    New vocabulary — My insults are now multilingual and creatively colorful, thanks to random voice chats.    Audio paranoia — Was that a footstep? A teammate reloading? Or just the wind? Either way, I’m pre-firing.    How to be yelled at in 4 languages — English, Russian, Arabic, and whatever dialect of rage my teammates invent on the spot.    Tactics over logic — 1v5? I got this. Bomb planted on B? Let’s rotate A just to confuse the enemy… and ourselves.    The art of gaslighting yourself — “I definitely hit that guy. 100% headshot. The server’s just broken.”    How to go from zen to psychotic in 3 rounds or less.    🧨 The CS2 Experience  You will:    Get queued with the nicest person ever... right before getting yelled at for buying a Negev on pistol round.    Watch your teammate jump into a molotov "for intel."    Die to a guy who hasn’t moved from spawn but somehow got a 4K with a deagle.    There’s something beautifully broken about it. It’s like a chaotic art project—equal parts genius and absurdity.    🎯 Skill Growth? Sure. Sanity? Debatable.  CS2 will make you better at FPS games. Your crosshair placement? Chef’s kiss. But occasionally, you’ll also find teammates who teach you smoke lineups, compliment your shots, or just vibe.    And those are the moments that remind you—this game is worth it.    🏁 Final Thoughts  CS2 isn’t just a game. It’s an experience. It’s equal parts punishment and dopamine, where you suffer with strangers and celebrate clutch moments like you just won a real war.    Whether you're rage-quitting, queueing again like a masochist, or proudly bottom-fragging with style, you're part of the wildest FPS community out there.    10/10 would get flashbanged by my own teammate again.

Valve, this wasn’t a bold new chapter—it was a botched facelift that buried one of the greatest shooters of all time. Rating: 7.5/10    TL;DR: CS2 is a visually impressive evolution of the Counter-Strike series, but the reduced drop system and increased monetization are drawbacks for casual players. If you’re a competitive fan, though, it’s still a solid experience.    Pros: New engine, improved visuals, great core gameplay, nostalgic feel, solid competitive experience.  Cons: Limited content at launch, monetization frustrations, drop system changes, occasional bugs.    Counter-Strike 2 (CS2) is the long-awaited evolution of CS:GO, taking the beloved tactical shooter into a new era with the Source 2 engine. With high hopes for modernizing the game and bringing it up to speed with current tech, it’s clear that CS2 is both a step forward and a bit of a step back in some areas. Let’s break it down:    New Engine: Visually Stunning, But…  The transition to the Source 2 engine brings a much-needed visual overhaul. Environments are more detailed, lighting is more dynamic, and gunplay feels smoother. The overall game looks sharper, and the physics are more immersive. For long-time players, it’s like seeing your favorite game in a new light — everything feels familiar but fresh. However, some players report performance issues on lower-end hardware, even with the improvements. It feels like they’ve pushed the engine to its limits, and while it works well on newer PCs, there are some hiccups for those running older setups.    Core Gameplay – Classic CS, But Sharper  At its core, CS2 maintains the tried-and-true mechanics that made CS:GO a staple in the esports world. The movement, shooting mechanics, and the overall feel of the game remain largely unchanged. Counter-Terrorists vs Terrorists, bomb planting, defusal — all the iconic modes and strategies are still intact.    However, some players feel like the game doesn’t feel as “polished” as it could be. It’s not that the game is bad — far from it — but the excitement of playing feels a little more restricted in terms of progression and rewards (more on that below). Still, if you’ve been a fan of the franchise, the gameplay will likely feel familiar and satisfying.    Content – A Little Sparse for Now  CS2 launched with fewer maps, skins, and features compared to the massive library of CS:GO. While new content is likely coming with updates, there’s a noticeable lack of variety at launch, especially when compared to the vast amount of skins and cases CS:GO accumulated over time. The reduced drop rate and the increased emphasis on microtransactions (with skins and cases) has left many players feeling like Valve is pushing a monetization-heavy approach to the game.    If you’re hoping to grind out some cases or earn a cool skin by playing casually, that’s going to be a lot harder in CS2 than it ever was in CS:GO, where you could get drops with every match. The transition to one case per week, tied to ranking up, has definitely rubbed a lot of players the wrong way.    Monetization – Pay to Play?  One of the biggest complaints about CS2 is its monetization. In CS:GO, you could get cases just by playing — and sell those cases or skins on the market for real money. CS2, however, seems to be following a more restrictive model. The one-case-per-week system and the higher cost of cases feel like Valve is leaning much harder into the pay-to-access model. Players who want to build a collection of skins or get a shot at rare items will either need to grind (but only get one drop per week) or pay a lot more money than in the past.    It feels like Valve is trying to find a balance between keeping the game free-to-play while still making money from skins, cases, and other premium content. The result? A less rewarding experience for players who used to enjoy collecting items through just playing the game.    Bugs & Stability  CS2 isn’t perfect yet. Despite being built on the newer Source 2 engine, some players report bugs, matchmaking issues, and occasional performance stuttering. Given Valve's history of gradually improving their games over time, it’s likely these problems will be ironed out in future patches, but it's something worth noting if you're diving into CS2 early.    The Competitive Scene  The competitive aspect of CS2 is where it really shines. Like its predecessors, CS2 is going to be a hit in the esports scene. The core mechanics, matchmaking system, and esports infrastructure all seem solid. The game retains its deep, skill-based gameplay that’s made it a favorite for pro players and competitive gamers alike. If you're in it for ranked matches, tournaments, and a high-skill environment, CS2 has everything you want — it’s just that the incentive to grind feels a lot lower than it did in CS:GO, where casual players could still get rewarded.    Final Thoughts  CS2 is undeniably a fantastic game in many ways. The visual overhaul is refreshing, the core gameplay remains solid, and the competitive scene is as strong as ever. However, the shift in the drop system and the emphasis on monetization are real downsides for a lot of players, especially those who loved the free-to-play, “grindy” nature of CS:GO.    If you're a competitive player, you're likely going to love the game, but for casual gamers who enjoyed the random drops, the grind for skins, and the excitement of earning rewards just by playing, CS2 may feel a bit like a cash grab.

Review: Counter-Strike 2 (CS2) – A Broken, Toxic Cash Grab  Counter-Strike 2 is less of a game and more of a poorly disguised money-laundering scheme wrapped in a barely functional FPS. Valve has taken everything wrong with modern gaming—exploitative microtransactions, a braindead playerbase, and incompetent development—and cranked it up to eleven. If you’re looking for a competitive shooter, look elsewhere. If you’re looking for a digital casino where idiots gamble away their paychecks on virtual guns, congratulations—you’ve found your game.   1. Skins: The Only Reason This Game Still Exists Let’s be real—nobody actually likes playing CS2. The only reason it still has players is because Valve has turned it into the world’s most elaborate skin gambling racket. The entire economy is built on:      Addicts overpaying for pixel guns because they think a neon AWP makes them better.     Third-world traders scamming kids out of their Steam wallets.     Money launderers using skins to move shady cash (because why use banks when you can trade a StatTrak Butterfly Knife      instead?).  Valve doesn’t care about gameplay—they care about taking a 15% cut every time some moron spends 2,000ona∗"FactoryNew"∗skinthatlooksidenticaltothe2,000ona∗"FactoryNew"∗skinthatlooksidenticaltothe5 version. The game itself is just the front for this unregulated, degenerate marketplace.   2. The Most Sensitive Playerbase in Existence The second you call someone "bad" or "gay" (which, historically, was half the fun of CS), they lose their minds. These fragile man-children will:      Report you for "toxicity" because their ego can’t handle banter.     Throw the match because you didn’t drop them a gun.     Cry in all-chat like they’re in a therapy session instead of a shooter.  CS used to be about thick skin and trash talk—now it’s filled with snowflakes who think competitive gaming should be a safe space.   3. Russian Bots Who Refuse to Communicate (or Think) EU matchmaking is a punishment straight out of a dystopian novel. Every game, you get:     Vodka-brained NPCs who only know how to scream "CYKA BLYAT" and rush mid like lemmings.     Spawn campers who sit in a corner with a shotgun, contributing nothing.     Players who refuse to speak English (but suddenly learn it when they need to flame you).  Valve’s non-existent region lock means you’re stuck with teammates who play like they’re using a Soviet-era calculator instead of a PC.    4. Shots Don’t Register, Hitboxes Are a Myth CS2’s "sub-tick" system is a scam. You’ll:     Headshot someone point-blank, see blood, and do zero damage.     Die behind walls because the netcode is held together by duct tape.     Lose every spray battle despite your crosshair being glued to the enemy.  Valve claims it’s *"better than 64-tick,"* but in reality, it’s worse than CS:GO’s worst community servers.    5. Cheaters Everywhere (and Valve Encourages It) VAC is a joke. Every match has:     Spinbotters who don’t even try to hide it.     Wallhackers who pre-fire you like they’re psychic.     Smurfs who queue with silvers just to stroke their ego.  Valve doesn’t care because cheaters = more accounts = more skin sales. Overwatch is dead, so the game is a free-for-all for script kiddies.   6. Maps Are Worse, Performance Is Garbage The "upgraded" maps somehow look uglier than CS:GO’s, with worse visibility and buggy smokes. Meanwhile, performance is worse despite looking almost identical. If you don’t have a $3,000 PC, enjoy stuttering and frame drops in every gunfight. Verdict: A Skinner Box Disguised as a Shooter   CS2 is not a game—it’s a psychological trap designed to keep addicts hooked on skin gambling while tolerating a broken, cheater-infested mess. The gameplay is worse, the community is insufferable, and Valve’s only priority is milking whales for every last dollar.  Rating: 1/10 – Only Play If You Hate Yourself

Players on Faceit are cheating with wallhacks, aimbots, and throwing games, while Valve? They’re doing nothing. But hey, it’s not just the bots and cheaters. Let’s talk about the servers. Every time you try to get into a match, it feels like you’re waiting for a miracle. The sv_  is so inconsistent, it’s like flipping a coin. You sit there waiting for 10 minutes just to see if you’ll get a decent server, while the rest of the players have ping ranges that look like a ping-pong match. Some people are sitting at 30ms, others are struggling at 100ms, and no one knows which server you’ll actually get — it’s a goddamn lottery at this point.  And what happens when you finally get in? Fix the cheaters, fix the bots, sort the damn servers, and stop overloading your maps. We’re tired of waiting 10 minutes for a decent server, dealing with 30ms for some players, and 100ms for others.  It’s 2025. Do your damn job.

Counter-Strike 2 is a thrilling evolution of the classic FPS franchise, blending tactical gunplay with a fast-paced multiplayer experience. Although known primarily as a competitive shooter, CS2 carries strong potential for players who enjoy RPG-like elements—team coordination, strategic planning, and progression in skill and ranking.  One of the most exciting aspects of CS2 is the vibrant community. Whether you're playing with old friends or meeting new ones, the social element adds an extra layer of enjoyment. The gameplay itself is highly engaging—bomb defusal missions, hostage rescues, and intense firefights all require quick thinking and coordination. Players who love tactical gunfights will find plenty of opportunities to apply strategy and teamwork.  Valve continues to update the game's maps and graphics, ensuring that the gameplay stays fresh and visually appealing. These updates reflect the developers' commitment to evolving the game alongside its player base.  On the downside, like many competitive online games, CS2 still faces challenges with cheating—such as wallhacks and aimbots. While this can affect the experience, it's important to acknowledge that the developers are actively working to improve anti-cheat measures and provide a fair environment for all players.  In conclusion, Counter-Strike 2 remains a top-tier multiplayer experience with deep tactical gameplay, a strong community, and ongoing development support. Despite some persistent issues with cheating, the overall quality and excitement of the game make it well worth playing.

echnical Issues and Performance Drops One of the most glaring problems with CS2 is its technical instability. CS:GO was known for its smooth performance, even on modest hardware, which made it accessible to a wide range of players. CS2, on the other hand, suffers from noticeable input lag, frame drops, and inconsistent hit registration—even on high-end systems. Competitive players, who rely on split-second precision, have found the new version unreliable, undermining the core tactical gameplay that made CS:GO a competitive eSports staple.  Removal of Key Features Rather than building upon CS:GO’s mature feature set, CS2 launched with several important elements missing. Casual and competitive modes were stripped down, beloved maps like Cache were absent, and core game mechanics—such as proper spray control—felt different or broken. Valve’s decision to ship CS2 as a full replacement for CS:GO rather than a parallel beta meant that millions were forced into a subpar experience with no alternative.  Poor Communication and Community Feedback Valve has long been criticized for its silence, but the rollout of CS2 amplified this issue. The community raised concerns about ranked matchmaking quality, VAC security, and a general lack of updates or meaningful developer communication. Unlike games that thrive on active community engagement (like Riot’s Valorant), CS2 has failed to establish a transparent roadmap or show responsiveness to user feedback. This has created a growing rift between the developers and the player base.  Questionable Design Decisions CS2’s overhauled smoke system, while technically impressive, has had mixed reception. Some players feel the new volumetric smokes break the flow of classic gunfights and enable unfair peeking tactics. In addition, weapon balance remains in flux, and some changes appear to have been made without considering long-term competitive viability. I would like to preface this by saying the following thoughts are based on my personal experience and perspective playing Counter-Strike 2's [CS:2] beta version. Counter-Strike: Global Offensive [CS:GO] has played a significant role in my life, and I offer these insights in the spirit of sharing my passion for Counter-Strike. As a player with over 8,000 hours invested in CS:GO since early 2014 and a past history in semi-professional play, with ~50 matches played on HLTV, my perspective may be influenced by my extensive time spent on CS:GO. I am now just a casual and washed-up player who plays with friends during my spare time.  I understand that the CS2 version is a limited-test, and not the full release. I have come into CS2 with an open mind and am fully aware that the game will still be in development and subject to changes. Therefore, I will discuss and evaluate CS2's current state compared to CS:GO.  Firstly, I'd like to consider some of the most important elements of CS:GO. While I won't delve into every aspect, I'll highlight key factors that can serve as reference points when discussing and evaluating CS2.  High Frame Rate and Optimised Graphics  CS:GO is optimised to run on a wide range of setups. We can often achieve fairly high and consistent frame rates on moderately powerful computers (with some optimisations). Further, CS:GO's graphics are finely tuned to strike a harmonious balance between visual quality and performance. This ensures that players with diverse setups can enjoy a seamless experience without compromising substantially on visual quality.  'Buttery Smooth' Feeling  Secondary to high frame rates, us players often describe the ideal CS:GO experience where everything feels exceptionally smooth, responsive, fast, and crisp. This is often attributed to other factors as well, including low-input lag and network infrastructure (i.e. 128-tick servers, responsive netcode, etc).  Movement  CS:GO's movement system feel intuitive, responsive, and quick. Character animations are smooth and fluid, allowing for advanced movements like bunny-hopping and strafing to feel seamless. This is a fundamental aspect of the game's competitive gameplay and contributes to the overall depth and skill ceiling of CS:GO.  There are many other factors which make CS:GO an elite first-person shooter game. However, after playing around 15 games of CS2, I can confidently state that there are numerous issues that need addressing.  Firstly, I think most can agree that performance is currently the biggest issue. The general consensus is that, even with optimisations, CS2 is not delivering with high and consistent frame rates. Although my PC is equipped to produce high frames, it is not able to constantly produce 300+ frames per second [fps] unlike CS:GO, which is producing 400 to 500 fps. I understand as games advance (i.e. Source 1 to Source 2 Engine) and technology evolves, the demand on hardware to deliver high frame rates and optimal performance will increase. CS2 is supposed to be an improved iteration of the game, yet it is marked by a concerning perception of poor performance. My gameplay experience should exhibit a smooth, swift, and crisp response, instead it feels noticeably delayed and lacks the fluidity and responsiveness expected. Further, there is noticeable stuttering and screen-tearing which feels like 60hz at times. Even though my system maintains a fairly high frame rate (i.e. 250 to 350 fps), the overall gameplay experience within CS2 resembles that of a considerably lower frame rate.  Secondly, it feels like the movement is quite 'sluggish'. I have switched between both CS:GO and CS:2 and the distinction is clear. The movement in CS2 is not yet refined to what Counter-Strike should feel like, and the input lag which is evident makes aiming and moving feel delayed. From swapping between the two games, it feels like 128-tick is much more responsive and elegant compared to the current sub-tick system. This might just be me, but the current sub-tick system feels like a cheap version of 128-tick. Additionally, I have noticed that player animations seem unnatural when enemies wide-swing/peak. There is undoubtedly an elevated advantage for players who peek first compared to CS:GO. This may be related to buggy character animations, lag compensation, interpolation, server-side issues, etc.  Thirdly, there is a clear issue with spraying when compared to CS:GO. Spraying feels somewhat random, and pulling down does not consistently produce the desired recoil control. I'm not sure if this is an intended change though.  Fourthly, the audio when hearing footsteps and other in-game noises sound unclear and can be quite difficult to differentiate. This may be a me problem, but I've heard this has been an issue for many other players too.  I have noticed some other minor issues, which include rubber-banding with nearby players, not being able to pick up weapons easily, difficulty noticing health drops, smoke duration being too long, and shots feeling delayed. I understand, and trust, that Valve will fix many of these issues (and others I have not mentioned). However, my concern lies around some of the discussed significant issues, especially considering that the game is expected to be fully released soon. In essence, my experience with CS:2 can be summarised with the age-old adage: "if it ain't broke, don't fix it." It underscores the importance of preserving the elements that have made Counter-Strike iconic while carefully considering necessary improvements for a seamless transition to the next chapter of the franchise.  I'm not here to take a dump on Valve or their CS2 efforts, but as a long-term player of Counter-Strike I believe it is vital to preserve the core elements that make Counter-Strike the best game in the world. Accepting suboptimal performance as the norm is not conducive to the longevity and health of the game. If this trajectory persists, there is a legitimate risk of the game permanently suffering from performance-related shortcomings. I understand that change is needed to keep the franchise fresh and appealing to new players and audiences. However, it is crucial that these changes are made with careful consideration of the game's identity and the expectations of its dedicated player base. Finding a balance between innovation and preserving the core essence of Counter-Strike is essential to ensure that the game continues to thrive and maintain its status as one of the most iconic games ever made.

🌟🌟🌟🌟☆ (4/5) – “CS2: Where My Aim Dies, and So Does My Faith in Humanity”    So I booted up Counter-Strike 2 thinking I’d relive the glory days of CS:GO—you know, crisp one-taps, clutch moments, and teammates who scream "EZ" after doing absolutely nothing. And in some ways, CS2 delivers. The gunplay still slaps harder than my WiFi during a storm, and the new graphics? Chef’s kiss. It’s like Valve gave the game a skincare routine—smooth, glowing, but still prone to breakouts (aka server lag).    Pros:    Gun sounds go BOOM and my serotonin goes YES.    Smokes are now physics-based, which means they can be bullied by bullets like me in Silver matchmaking.    Movement feels slick, unless you're trying to bhop, in which case: condolences.    New UI is clean, except I still panic-buy an auto instead of armor, but that’s on me.    Cons:    Cheaters. CHEATERS. I don’t know who hurt them in life, but every other game has some dude pretending to be a level 3 wizard casting headshots through walls.    VAC is about as vigilant as a mall cop on break. I’ve reported players more times than I’ve clutched 1v5s (read: once, but it was a good one).    Matchmaking sometimes feels like it’s trying to teach me humility. "Oh, you won a game? Here’s a teammate who thinks 'planting the bomb' means yoga."    Do I recommend it? Yes—if you’ve got the patience of a saint and a sense of humor about losing. It’s chaotic, sweaty, rage-inducing fun. Just keep your expectations realistic: you're not climbing the ranks, you're surviving them.    Final thoughts: CS2 is like an ex you keep going back to. You know it’s toxic, you know you’ll be mad, but man… when it’s good? It’s so, so good.

Solid game. It's fun to play with friends. The reason I don't recommend it is because getting into the game is pretty difficult. There's a big learning curve at the start, which is frustrating. Understanding maps, spray control, movement, and other mechanics takes much longer in this game compared to similar tactical shooters. It's also missing some quality-of-life features. I'll compare it to Valorant, which has a significantly better minimap system. It shows where your teammates see enemies, marks smoke areas, and more. Valorant also doesn't require counter-strafing, and its bullet tracers are more visible, which helps you learn recoil control more easily. The shooting in this game feels hard to control. As a new player, I often couldn't tell where my bullets were going or if I was accurate. Over time, you build some muscle memory and gun control gets better, but I think the difficulty is unnecessary. Once you get the hang of it, I can see it being fun. But if you're unsure about getting this game, I’d suggest going with Valorant instead.

It's... fine, I guess?  So, I've put a decent number of hours into CS2 now, and honestly? It’s a bit of a mixed bag.  Visually, the game looks way better than CS:GO. The updated maps, lighting, and effects (especially the new smoke mechanics) are cool. You can tell they really tried to modernize the look without losing that classic CS feel. But that’s kinda where the smooth ride ends.  The new sub-tick system sounds great on paper, but in practice, things feel off sometimes. Hit reg can be inconsistent, and the movement doesn't feel as crisp as CS:GO. Some fights just feel weird, like you hit your shots but nothing connects. It’s hard to describe unless you’ve played both a lot.  Performance-wise, it’s been rough. I’ve got a decent rig, but I still get random stutters and FPS drops, especially in certain maps. And don’t even get me started on the occasional crashes.  Matchmaking is better structured with the new Premier mode, but there are still a lot of cheaters slipping through. VAC Live sounds promising, but it doesn’t feel like it’s doing much just yet.  I want to love CS2, and maybe in 6–12 months I will. Right now, though, it feels more like a visual upgrade with some questionable changes rather than a true next-gen leap.  Verdict: It's still Counter-Strike, but it needs time to grow. “CS2: A Game Held Hostage – A Veteran’s Cry by Jermery Ganga” By Jermery Ganga, 37 years old. Former Silver Elite Master. Now full-time matchmaker punching bag. Survivor of Overwatch cases. Holder of grudges since Source.  🎧 Prologue: What Have They Done to My Boy? When Counter-Strike 2 came knocking, I opened the door like a dad greeting his prodigal son. I expected growth, maybe a new haircut, maybe an extra tattoo. What I got instead? A glossier face, a fake smile, and a knife behind the back.  I’ve played Counter-Strike since I could barely afford a Logitech mouse. CS was never about flash — it was about tension, timing, and knowing that if you died, it was your fault. CS2? Well… now I get headshot through smokes by a guy whose profile has anime, VAC ban, and 12 hours in the past two weeks.  🕹️ Gameplay: Smooth Gunfights in a Dirty Battlefield Gunplay feels nice, I'll admit. There’s a new weight to shots, a modern zip to movement. Peeking feels faster. AK recoil is crisp.  But the improvements only matter when the game is fair — and lately, it rarely is.  On a good day, CS2 feels like a refined CS:GO.  On a bad day? It’s like dueling someone with a water pistol while they’ve got an aimbot installed on their Tesla.  Volumetric smokes still look cool. Still impractical in high-pressure scenarios. You can shoot through them. You can blow them up. But no matter what you do, you can’t stop cheaters from walking out of them headshotting you with perfect pre-aim.  💻 Cheating: The Rot in the Core Let me be clear:  Cheating in CS2 is the worst I’ve seen since 2009.  Every other match has at least one player who thinks toggling walls at halftime is “subtle.”  Spinbots? Yup, still there.  Wallhacks? Constant.  Aimbots with “humanized” delay? They stare at the floor until your head peaks.  Scripted jumps, no-flash macros, auto-strafers — it’s like every round is an episode of Black Mirror: FPS Edition.  And the worst part?  VAC doesn’t care.  I’ve reported the same cheater three times over a week. He’s still playing. Still griefing.  Prime status doesn’t mean anything anymore — just means they paid five bucks to smurf harder.  Matchmaking is a warzone without rules. Half the lobbies feel like cheat developers testing new builds.  When I queue into Premier and see a guy with 5 kills and 15 headshots, I don’t scream anymore. I just sigh. Because I know Jermery Ganga is not fighting players anymore — he’s fighting algorithms coded by Russian teenagers.  🎨 Visuals & Maps: Pretty, But Pointless in Hell The maps are beautiful. I’ll give Valve credit — Source 2 turned Dust II into an architectural thesis. Mirage is sleek. Inferno glows.  But when cheaters know every pixel angle and flick through walls with surgical precision, beauty becomes background noise.  Lighting has made visibility worse in some cases — and when you mix that with cheaters abusing contrast and ESP overlays, it feels like I’m fighting invisible gods with a blindfold on.  🧠 Culture, Spirit & Fatigue CS2 has the bones of greatness — I feel it when I hit a clean flick, or win a 1v2. But the soul is fading.  Players are burned out. Half my friends list doesn’t queue anymore.  Trust factor is broken. VACnet is silent. Third-party platforms are the last safe haven.  I didn’t come to CS2 to be gaslit every round. I came here to clutch, choke, cheer, and scream. Instead, I feel like I’m beta-testing a broken carnival ride built by ghosts.  🔚 Final Words: 6/10 – A Game With a Knife in Its Back If CS2 was a man, I’d sit him down, hand him a beer, and say:  “You’ve got potential, kid. But you’ve surrounded yourself with the worst people alive.”  This game needs a reckoning. Not a new crate, not a new skin — a purge. Until cheating is addressed, every win feels hollow, every loss suspicious, and every highlight tainted.  But still… I queue. Because I’m Jermery Ganga. And I remember what it felt like to ace a bombsite when it meant something.  Valve — if you’re listening:  Fix the cheating, or the legacy you built will become a tombstone we all camp behind.

Counter-Strike 2   As someone who's played csgo on and off over the years I was both curious and cautious going into Counter-Strike 2. After putting in a decent amount of hours, I can say it’s definitely a step forward in some areas  though it’s not without its flaws.  What Stands Out:  The visual overhaul is the first thing you’ll notice. Maps feel cleaner and more polished, with better lighting and details thanks to the Source 2 engine. The new smoke effects are a cool touch and actually change how certain situations play out tactically.  Gunplay is still the heart of the game, and thankfully, it still feels sharp and satisfying. Movement, aiming, and shooting all retain that signature Counter-Strike precision. It’s familiar, but with a bit more polish.  The new UI looks slick, and I found matchmaking to be a bit more consistent compared to CS:GO — though maybe that’s just good luck.  Some Downsides:  Performance hasn’t been perfect. At launch, I ran into a few bugs and random FPS drops that weren’t present in CS:GO. It’s better now after a couple of updates, but it still needs a bit more optimization.  Also, if you're new to Counter Strike, the game doesn’t do much to ease you in. It’s just as punishing as ever for beginners, and I wish there were more tools or modes to help newer players get comfortable.  Finally, some people expected more content out of the gate  more maps, more noticeable changes. Right now, it feels more like a big upgrade to CS:GO rather than a whole new game.  Final Thoughts:  Overall, Counter-Strike 2 is a solid update that keeps the core gameplay intact while giving it a modern shine. If you already enjoy CS:GO, you’ll probably appreciate what’s here. If you’re completely new, it might take some time to click  but for those willing to put in the effort, there’s a rewarding game underneath.
